notes.1: Candidates found this first question one of the most accessible questions on this paper and did reasonably well on it. They especially did very well on (d) and (i). Candidates struggled on (c).
notes.1a: There were a wide range of incorrect answers here. Many candidates chose metals as their answer with the most common incorrect answer being ‘calcium’.
notes.1b: Many candidates could not identify ‘an ionic compound’. ‘Carbon dioxide’ and ‘sulfur dioxide’ were common incorrect answers.
notes.1c: Candidates struggled with this question part and did not know that it was a transition metal.
notes.1d: This question was very well answered.
notes.1e: This question was very well answered. The only candidates who did not get this one correct were those that got (d) and (e) confused.
notes.1f: Many candidates did not know the reactivity series of metals and so thought the answer to this was ‘calcium’ or ‘aluminium’.
notes.1g: Candidates struggled with this chemical test recall question.
notes.1h: This question was very well answered.
notes.1i: Most candidates could answer this question correctly.
notes.2: Candidates found this question more challenging than the previous one and it discriminated very well between candidates. Candidates particularly found (b) and (e) challenging.
notes.2a: (i) Most candidates could state the correct chemical name from the formula given. However, there were a few candidates that incorrectly thought that the chemical name was ‘magnesium sulfite’ or ‘magnesium sulfur oxide’.
notes.2aii: Most candidates could work out the correct answer for this calculation using the data given. There were a few candidates that got the data mixed up and so did not gain credit. Some candidates were a factor of 10 or 100 out.
notes.2iii: Most candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.2b: Candidates found this question very challenging and could not recall the chemical test for bromide ions. Some candidates got confused with other chemical tests. A few candidates put the correct reagent but then the wrong colour of precipitate.
notes.2c: Many candidates could show the correct electronic configuration of a calcium ion. Not as many knew the correct charge on this ion.
notes.2d: Candidates found this ‘kinetic particle model’ question much harder. In quite a few cases they misinterpreted the rubric. Some candidates got the terms ‘arrangement’ and ‘separation’ confused and wrote down a correct answer for separation and not arrangement. Candidates also wrongly compared states. They talked about ways of changing the state of the solid and so did not achieve any credit. In many cases candidates confused bulk properties with particle movement. Lots of candidates described incorrectly the speed or distance between the particles.
notes.2e: Candidates struggled with this question and found it very challenging. Many candidates did not know ‘one source of nitrate ions’. ‘Cars’ and ‘rivers’ were examples of incorrect answers.
notes.3: Candidates found this question about phosphorus and its compounds much easier. They particularly did well on (a)(ii) and (iii) but found (a)(iv) challenging.
notes.3a: (i) This question was not well answered by many candidates. Many candidates did not know why phosphorus is in Group V of the Periodic Table.
notes.3aii: Candidates did better on this question. Most knew how to work out the number of protons present in each isotope and could give the correct answers. Some struggled with the number of neutrons and electrons and some got these mixed up.
notes.3iii: A very well answered question. Most candidates could correctly balance the given equation.
notes.3iv: Candidates found this question very challenging. Many incorrectly thought that phosphorus(V) oxide was a basic oxide.
notes.3b: (i) Most candidates answered this question correctly. The most common incorrect answer was ‘krypton’.
notes.3bii: This question was very well answered. The most common correct answers were ‘for faster plant growth’ and ‘to increase the yield’.
notes.3c: Candidates struggled to calculate the relative formula mass of the given compound and there were many incorrect answers seen. Instead of using the number of atoms in the given formula, a lot of candidates used the atomic number of the element which gave, incorrectly, very big numbers for the answer.
notes.4: This question discriminated well between candidates. Candidates were able to identify uses of the petroleum products in (a)(iii). However, they found (a)(ii) very challenging and struggled to answer the longer question on the separation of petroleum.
notes.4a: (i) This question was not very well answered. Candidates could not recall the meaning of the term hydrocarbon. Many candidates could state part of the definition but not all of it. Most omitted the words ‘compound’ or ‘only’ which were needed to gain credit.
notes.4aii: Candidates struggled with this four mark question on the separation of petroleum. Few candidates gained full credit. Many candidates thought that the separation technique incorrectly was ‘cracking’ or ‘filtration’. Not many candidates knew that for the hydrocarbons to be separated in this way they have to have different boiling points.
notes.4iii: Most candidates answered this uses question correctly. This was an improvement on previous years where candidates had struggled with the uses of substances in the fractional distillation of petroleum.
notes.4b: (i) Candidates struggled to ‘draw the displayed formula of a molecule of ethanol’. Lots of incorrect answers were seen, including the incorrect number of carbon atoms. Some candidates omitted to put the covalent bond between the oxygen and hydrogen of the alcohol functional group. Many candidates did not attempt this question.
notes.4bii: Candidates found this question very challenging. Many candidates did not know at least one condition for the manufacture of ethanol using steam and ethene. Many candidates incorrectly used conditions from the fermentation process instead.
notes.4c: (i) Most candidates were able to deduce the molecular formula of the given compound correctly.
notes.4cii: Most candidates answered this question correctly and could easily identify the two elements in tetramethylsilane that were in the same group in the Periodic Table.
notes.5: This question discriminated very well between candidates. Candidates found (a)(iii) and (c) very challenging. They did not know how to make crystals of the pure salt from an aqueous solution of it. Candidates also struggled with the meaning of the term ‘ionic bond’.
notes.5a: (i) Most candidates answered this question correctly. However, some candidates thought that ‘carbon dioxide’ or ‘hydrogen’ was given off instead of ‘water’.
notes.5aii: Candidates found this question more challenging. Common incorrect answers were ‘distillation’ and ‘evaporation’.
notes.5iii: This question discriminated very well between candidates. Many candidates could name the product formed at each electrode. Some got ‘chloride’ confused with the correct ‘chlorine’. A few candidates misread the question and thought that the electrolysis was in aqueous solution and so used hydrogen as one of their answers.
notes.5b: (i) Many candidates could correctly label the ‘electrolyte’ and the ‘cathode’. However, some did label the wires instead which was incorrect.
notes.5bii: Some candidates found this question challenging and did not give a suitable material. Common incorrect answers were ‘copper’ and ‘aluminium’.
notes.5c: Many candidates did not know the meaning of the term ‘ionic bond’.
notes.6: Candidates did well on some parts of this question especially (a)(i) and (c)(i). However, some candidates struggled to suggest one property of the given alloy as in (c)(iii).
notes.6a: (i) The majority of candidates were able to answer this question correctly. This was the question on this paper that had the highest amount of completely correct answers.
notes.6aii: Candidates found this question very challenging especially as it was asking for two ways to decrease the rate of the given reaction. Many candidates just talked about decreasing the amount of metal or volume of hydrochloric acid used which was incorrect.
notes.6b: Many candidates did not know the correct flame colour for potassium ions.
notes.6c: (i) Most candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.6cii: Most candidates could name one of the correct metals in this question. This was usually copper. However, the second metal caused more problems. Lots of different metals and compounds were seen especially aluminium, steel, iron and tin.
notes.6iii: Candidates struggled on this question. There were very few correct answers seen. ‘High melting point’ or ‘conducts electricity’ were the most common incorrect answers.
notes.7: Candidates performed well on this question and found it quite straight forward. They especially found (b) and
notes.7c: (i) Most candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.7a: Most candidates could select at least one of the chemical changes in this question.
notes.7b: The majority of candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.7cii: Candidates found this question slightly more challenging. The most common incorrect answer was Experiment 4 where candidates got mixed up with the temperature changes for an exothermic and an endothermic reaction.
notes.7iii: Most candidates answered this question correctly. The most common incorrect answer was ‘2H’ instead of ‘H ’.
notes.7iv: Candidates found this question more challenging. While most candidates could label the ‘reactants’ and ‘products’ the correct way, many did not know the name of the ‘vertical axis’.
notes.8: Candidates found this question the hardest one on the paper. They particularly struggled with questions on flue gas desulfurisation and testing whether a sample of water is pure using melting point in (c)(ii) and (b). They did better on the treatment of domestic water and its stages in (a).
notes.8a: Most candidates answered this question correctly.
notes.8b: Candidates found this question very challenging and there were very few completely correct answers. The most common incorrect answer was candidates referring to the boiling point of pure water instead of the melting point. Many candidates did not know the melting point of pure water.
notes.8c: (i) Candidates struggled with this question and many did not know one harmful effect of the given air pollutants. Some candidates just put down ‘harmful’, which was given in the stem of the question.
notes.8cii: Very few candidates gave a completely correct answer here. A few candidates knew correctly that flue gas desulfurisation was a neutralisation reaction.

notes.general_comments:
Many candidates tackled this paper well, showing a good knowledge of core chemistry. Good answers were
seen throughout the paper across a range of different questions. Most candidates found parts of every
question challenging. Nearly all candidates were entered at the appropriate level. It was evident that many
candidates are now using past paper practice as part of their revision programme, but more revision is
needed on some aspects of this syllabus.
